top_story: As the 60-day understanding around the Strait of Hormuz lapsed on 17 August, Trump escalated from demanding Iran’s surrender to threatening Oman if Muscat impeded a US-Iran arrangement, sharpening pressure on a state that has long served as a critical Gulf intermediary. That coercive turn compounds a wider war shock already hitting civilian life and regional commerce, with Middle Eastern airlines now facing a projected $4.3 billion loss in 2026 as insecurity suppresses travel, disrupts routes, and slows postwar recovery. In parallel, Jared Kushner’s contacts in Egypt with Hamas and his subsequent talks with Netanyahu produced no movement on Gaza, because Israel still conditions any deal on Hamas disarmament and rejects troop withdrawal beforehand. The emerging picture is of a region where coercive diplomacy is narrowing mediating space while conflict spillover deepens economic damage and leaves core political negotiations frozen.
